error_modes.label: EMERGENCY AIRFIELD SELECTION AND HEADING/TIME/FUEL PLANNING FROM TURNING POINTS

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete study of the route during mission planning, did not choose emergency airfields for the legs of the navigation and produced no heading, time or fuel figures from the turning points to the nearest suitable field. When asked in flight for the nearest emergency airfield and the fuel required to reach it, SP had no answer and no method to derive one. The IP had to supply the field, the heading and the fuel figure and to direct the aircraft, and the emergency airfield portion of the sortie was flown by the IP.
texts.1: SP, due to planning that covered only the departure and destination fields, carried emergency airfield data for part of the route only and the heading, time and fuel figures from the remaining turning points were missing. The gaps were filled in flight only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP and the figures were produced late, with errors at the limit of what remains acceptable. SP arrived at a usable answer for each turning point, but only under direct questioning rather than as part of the plan.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried final check of the flight plan, initially quoted the heading and fuel to the emergency airfield from the wrong turning point. SP recognized the discrepancy from the elapsed time and the fuel remaining, reworked the figures without any prompting and passed the corrected heading, time and fuel for the correct field. The error stayed within minor limits and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP chose appropriate emergency airfields for every leg of the route and planned correctly, with minor errors only, the heading, time and fuel from each turning point to the nearest emergency airfield. The figures were available immediately on request in flight and were consistent with the actual fuel state and winds. SP updated them as the sortie progressed.
texts.4: SP selected emergency airfields that matched the route, the weather and the aircraft performance, and had accurate heading, time and fuel from every turning point ready without reference to notes. The figures were revised in flight against actual groundspeed and fuel flow, so the divert picture stayed current at all times. Every answer given to the IP matched the aircraft state precisely.
texts.marginal: SP planned emergency airfields and had heading, time and fuel available for each turning point within the required standards, but the figures were static and were not revised as actual winds and fuel flow diverged from the plan. The trend was toward quoting planned numbers rather than current ones. SP is expected to keep the divert figures updated in flight so that they remain valid at the moment they are needed.

texts_at.1: SP planned emergency airfields and the heading, time and fuel from each turning point inside the standard required at this stage, the figures for one turning point produced only under direct questioning rather than as part of the plan. The trend traces to planning covering the departure and destination fields in detail but the intermediate turning points only lightly. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to plan every turning point to the same depth as the departure and destination so the figures are ready without questioning.
texts_at.2: SP planned emergency airfields and the heading, time and fuel from each turning point inside the standard required at this stage, one heading and fuel figure initially quoted from the wrong turning point during a hurried final check. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the flight plan without hurrying so the figures are correct on the first read.
texts_at.3: SP chose appropriate emergency airfields for every leg and planned the heading, time and fuel from each turning point with only minor errors, figures available immediately on request, the small margin tracing to one update lagging the actual fuel state by a beat. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to update every figure at the same pace as the fuel state so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the discrepancy from the elapsed time and the fuel remaining, reworked the figures without prompting and passed the corrected heading, time and fuel for the correct field, after initially quoting the wrong turning point during a hurried check. Checking the flight plan without hurrying from the start, rather than recognizing the discrepancy afterward, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good emergency airfield planning.
texts_above.3: SP chose appropriate emergency airfields for every leg of the route and planned correctly, with minor errors only, the heading, time and fuel from each turning point to the nearest emergency airfield, figures available immediately on request and updated as the sortie progressed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good emergency airfield planning.
texts_above.4: SP selected emergency airfields that matched the route, the weather and the aircraft performance, accurate heading, time and fuel from every turning point ready without reference to notes and revised in flight against actual groundspeed and fuel flow. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent emergency airfield planning.

error_modes.label: USE OF AIRCRAFT PERFORMANCE CHARTS FROM THE CHECK LIST

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient familiarity with the performance section of the Check List, was unable to extract the required performance data for the planned profile and used remembered figures instead of the charts. The fuel and range values applied to the route were not supported by any chart entry and did not match the aircraft configuration or the ambient conditions. The IP had to work the charts and provide the correct figures before the navigation could be flown as planned.
texts.1: SP, due to entering the performance charts with the wrong pressure altitude and temperature, derived fuel flow and range figures that did not match the actual conditions. The error was identified and reworked only after the IP pointed out the mismatch between the planned and the observed fuel consumption. The corrected figures were obtained at the limit of the time available and were accepted with errors at the edge of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to reading the wrong column of the cruise performance chart, initially set a power setting that gave a fuel flow higher than planned. SP noticed the discrepancy at the first turning point fuel check, returned to the Check List, re-entered the chart correctly and reset the cruise parameters. The excursion in fuel used stayed short of the planned reserve margin and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP used the aircraft performance charts from the Check List correctly, entering them with the actual pressure altitude, temperature and weight, and applied the resulting cruise, range and fuel figures to the navigation. Chart extraction was quick and the values were consistent with the observed fuel flow in flight.
texts.4: SP moved through the Check List performance charts without hesitation, interpolated correctly between chart entries and produced cruise, range and endurance figures that matched the observed aircraft performance almost exactly. SP re-entered the charts when conditions changed and confirmed the fuel plan against them before each leg.
texts.marginal: SP extracted the correct figures from the Check List performance charts and stayed within the required standards, but chart entry was slow and required more than one attempt when interpolation was involved. The trend was toward the chart work absorbing capacity that the navigation task also demanded. SP is expected to practice chart extraction until the figures can be produced accurately at first attempt.

texts_at.1: SP used the aircraft performance charts from the Check List inside the standard required at this stage, fuel flow and range figures reworked only after the IP pointed out a mismatch with the observed consumption. The trend traces to the chart being entered with an assumed pressure altitude and temperature rather than the actual values. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to enter the chart with the actual pressure altitude and temperature every time so the figures do not need reworking.
texts_at.2: SP used the aircraft performance charts from the Check List inside the standard required at this stage, one power setting initially read from the wrong column of the cruise chart before the discrepancy was noticed at the first fuel check. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the chart column before setting power so the discrepancy does not reach the first fuel check.
texts_at.3: SP used the aircraft performance charts from the Check List correctly, entering them with the actual pressure altitude, temperature and weight, chart extraction quick and consistent with the observed fuel flow, the small margin tracing to one interpolation taking a moment longer than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to practice that interpolation so it matches the pace of the rest of the chart work.

texts_above.2: SP noticed the discrepancy at the first turning point fuel check, returned to the Check List, re-entered the chart correctly and reset the cruise parameters, the excursion in fuel used staying short of the planned reserve margin with no IP input. Confirming the chart column before setting power, rather than noticing the discrepancy at the first fuel check, would remove even that excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound performance chart usage.
texts_above.3: SP used the aircraft performance charts from the Check List correctly, entering them with the actual pressure altitude, temperature and weight and applying the resulting cruise, range and fuel figures to the navigation, extraction quick and consistent with observed fuel flow in flight. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed performance chart usage.
texts_above.4: SP moved through the Check List performance charts without hesitation, interpolated correctly between chart entries and produced cruise, range and endurance figures that matched observed aircraft performance almost exactly. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional performance chart usage.

error_modes.label: USE OF AERONAUTICAL CHARTS AND MAPS FOR ORIENTATION

texts.0: SP, due to an inability to relate the aeronautical chart to the terrain, could not identify the planned checkpoints and could not fix the aircraft position on the map at any point of the leg. Chart handling in the cockpit was disorganized, with the wrong sheet and the wrong scale in use for the segment being flown. Orientation was lost, the aircraft tracked well outside the planned route, and the IP took control to re-establish position and recover the navigation.
texts.1: SP, due to reading the chart in isolation from the terrain features actually visible, misidentified a checkpoint and continued on a track that did not correspond to the planned leg. Position was re-established on the chart only after the IP directed attention to the correct feature, and the resulting track error reached the limit of the acceptable standard. SP was able to use the chart, but only with verbal guidance on what to look for.
texts.2: SP, due to folding the chart so that the next segment was not immediately visible, was slow to confirm the second checkpoint and allowed a small track offset to develop. SP refolded the chart, re-identified the feature against the terrain and corrected back to the planned track without any prompting. The offset remained well inside the standard and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP used the aeronautical charts and maps correctly throughout, keeping the appropriate sheet and scale available for the segment in use and identifying every planned checkpoint against the terrain. Position was fixed on the chart continuously and the chart work did not interfere with aircraft control or lookout.
texts.4: SP handled the aeronautical charts with complete fluency, anticipating each checkpoint from the chart before it appeared and confirming it against the terrain as it did. Position on the chart was known at every moment of the route, including during turns and configuration changes, and chart management consumed no measurable capacity from flying the aircraft.
texts.marginal: SP used the aeronautical charts and identified all checkpoints within the required standards, but chart handling in the cockpit was cumbersome and each fix required a prolonged head-down period. The trend was toward the map work competing with the lookout and the instrument scan. SP is expected to organize the chart before flight so that each segment can be confirmed with a short, deliberate reference.

texts_at.1: SP used aeronautical charts and maps for orientation inside the standard required at this stage, position on the chart re-established only after the IP directed attention to the correct feature. The trend traces to the chart being read in isolation from the terrain features actually visible rather than cross-checked against them continuously. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to cross-check the chart against visible terrain continuously so a misidentified checkpoint is caught without direction.
texts_at.2: SP used aeronautical charts and maps for orientation inside the standard required at this stage, a small track offset developing while the chart was folded so the next segment was not immediately visible. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to fold the chart to show the next segment before it is needed so the offset does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP used the aeronautical charts and maps correctly throughout, keeping the appropriate sheet and scale available and identifying every planned checkpoint against the terrain, position fixed continuously, the small margin tracing to one fix taking a beat longer than the rest during a configuration change. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to fix position at the same pace regardless of configuration changes so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP refolded the chart, re-identified the feature against the terrain and corrected back to the planned track without prompting, the offset staying well inside the standard, after a small track offset had developed while the chart was folded incorrectly. Folding the chart to show the next segment before it is needed, rather than refolding after an offset develops, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid chart and map handling.
texts_above.3: SP used the aeronautical charts and maps correctly throughout, keeping the appropriate sheet and scale available for the segment in use and identifying every planned checkpoint against the terrain, position fixed on the chart continuously without interfering with aircraft control or lookout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed chart and map handling.
texts_above.4: SP handled the aeronautical charts with complete fluency, anticipating each checkpoint from the chart before it appeared and confirming it against the terrain as it did, position known at every moment including during turns and configuration changes. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding chart and map handling.

error_modes.label: ANTICIPATION OF No1 INTENTIONS AS WINGMAN WITHOUT ASSUMING

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete mental model of the navigation sequence that was not updated when No1 changed the plan, acted on an assumed intention instead of the briefed and transmitted one. SP initiated a turn and a descent that No1 had not called and that did not correspond to the route being flown, and did not query No1 at any point. Formation integrity and separation were compromised and the IP took control to reposition the aircraft and restore the correct sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to retaining the briefed mental model after No1 had amended the leg, anticipated the wrong action and was late in following the actual maneuver. The correct intention was established only after No1 and the IP prompted verbally, and the resulting position error reached the limit of the acceptable standard. SP followed No1 correctly thereafter, but only after being told what was intended rather than by confirming it.
texts.2: SP, due to a mental model that briefly lagged the change of turning point, began to anticipate the previously briefed heading. SP recognized the mismatch against the chart and the formation geometry, asked No1 to confirm the intention rather than assuming it, and repositioned in time. The deviation stayed short of the standard limit and required no IP input.
texts.3: SP anticipated No1's intentions correctly throughout the navigation, positioning early for turns, descents and configuration changes, and never acted on an assumption. Where the intention was not clear, SP asked and confirmed before acting, and the formation sequence was maintained without prompting.
texts.4: SP read No1's intentions accurately in advance at every stage of the route, so each turn, speed change and descent was anticipated and matched without delay. SP verified rather than assumed on every occasion of ambiguity, using short and precise cross-talk, and the formation flowed through the navigation without a single corrective call from No1 or the IP.
texts.marginal: SP anticipated No1's intentions and stayed within the required standards, but anticipation was based more on the expected pattern than on the calls actually made and was not confirmed when the sequence changed. The trend was toward assuming rather than verifying. SP is expected to keep the mental model aligned with No1 by confirming the intention whenever the plan departs from the brief.

texts_at.1: SP anticipated No1's intentions as wingman without assuming inside the standard required at this stage, the correct intention established only after No1 and the IP prompted verbally. The trend traces to the briefed mental model being retained after No1 had amended the leg rather than updated with the change. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to update the mental model the moment a change is heard so the correct intention does not need prompting.
texts_at.2: SP anticipated No1's intentions as wingman without assuming inside the standard required at this stage, briefly anticipating the previously briefed heading while the mental model lagged a change of turning point. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the mental model against the chart at every turning point change so it does not lag.
texts_at.3: SP anticipated No1's intentions correctly throughout the navigation, positioning early for turns, descents and configuration changes and never acting on an assumption, the small margin tracing to one confirmation being requested a beat after the anticipated action rather than before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm before anticipating on every occasion so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the mismatch against the chart and the formation geometry, asked No1 to confirm the intention rather than assuming it, and repositioned in time, the deviation staying short of the standard limit after briefly anticipating a previously briefed heading. Checking the mental model against the chart at every turning point change, rather than recognizing the lag afterward, would remove even that mismatch. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady wingman anticipation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated No1's intentions correctly throughout the navigation, positioning early for turns, descents and configuration changes and never acting on an assumption, asking and confirming whenever the intention was not clear. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate wingman anticipation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP read No1's intentions accurately in advance at every stage of the route, each turn, speed change and descent anticipated and matched without delay, verifying rather than assuming on every occasion of ambiguity with short and precise cross-talk. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary wingman anticipation discipline.

error_modes.label: ORIENTATION AND CONTROL/PERFORMANCE CROSS-CHECK DURING THE ROUTE

texts.0: SP, due to a breakdown of the cross-check between the control and performance instruments and the outside references, stopped correlating the aircraft position with the planned route and lost orientation on the leg. Heading, altitude and timing were left unmonitored for an extended period and no correction was attempted. The aircraft tracked outside the planned corridor and below the briefed minimum altitude, and the IP took control to re-establish the route.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention stayed on the map, failed to detect a developing heading and altitude trend on the leg. Orientation with respect to the planned track was restored only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP, and the resulting track and altitude excursion reached the limit of the acceptable standard. The correction, once applied, was in the right sense but late.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that narrowed onto the outside references while identifying a checkpoint, delayed detection of a developing heading and altitude trend. SP recognized the deviation without prompting, restored the full cross-check and corrected back onto the planned track and altitude. The excursion stayed between the acceptable and the limiting values and required no IP input.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside references and kept accurate orientation with respect to the planned route throughout. Deviations in heading, altitude and timing were identified as trends and corrected promptly, with tasks prioritized correctly during map work and radio calls.
texts.4: SP kept an uninterrupted scan across the control instruments, the performance instruments and the terrain, and correlated aircraft position with the planned route continuously. Trends were recognized before they became deviations, so corrections were small and the aircraft stayed on the planned track, altitude and timing for the whole route.
texts.marginal: SP kept orientation and held the route parameters within the required standards, but the cross-check narrowed noticeably each time map work or a radio call was added. The trend was toward detecting deviations only after they were established rather than as trends. SP is expected to keep the scan open under load and to act on the trend rather than on the resulting error.

texts_at.1: SP kept orientation and cross-checked control and performance instruments against outside references inside the standard required at this stage, the track and altitude excursion reaching the limit of the acceptable standard before repeated prompting from the IP. The trend traces to the cross-check being interrupted while attention stayed on the map rather than continued alongside it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the cross-check running while reading the map so trends are detected before they reach the limit.
texts_at.2: SP kept orientation and cross-checked control and performance instruments against outside references inside the standard required at this stage, detection of a developing heading and altitude trend delayed while the scan narrowed onto outside references during a checkpoint identification. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the instrument scan open during checkpoint identification so the trend is detected without delay.
texts_at.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside references and kept accurate orientation throughout, deviations identified as trends and corrected promptly, the small margin tracing to one correction during radio work being a beat slower than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same correction speed during radio work so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the deviation without prompting, restored the full cross-check and corrected back onto the planned track and altitude, the excursion staying between the acceptable and the limiting values, after the scan had narrowed onto outside references during a checkpoint identification. Keeping the instrument scan open during checkpoint identification from the start, rather than restoring it after a delay, would remove even that excursion. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable orientation cross-check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the control and performance instruments against the outside references and kept accurate orientation with respect to the planned route throughout, deviations in heading, altitude and timing identified as trends and corrected promptly. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good orientation cross-check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP kept an uninterrupted scan across the control instruments, the performance instruments and the terrain, correlating aircraft position with the planned route continuously so trends were recognized before they became deviations. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior orientation cross-check discipline.

error_modes.label: TASK PRIORITIZATION AND SATURATION IN THE NAVIGATION COCKPIT

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated map reading, log keeping, radio work and the fuel check inside the same turning point, saturated and stopped flying the aircraft as the first priority. Tasks were dropped rather than shed in a deliberate order, the turn was flown without reference to heading and the required calls were missed. The aircraft state deteriorated beyond the acceptable limits and the IP took control to unload the cockpit and restore the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to attempting the fuel check, the log entry and the position report simultaneously at the turning point, allowed attention to channelize on the log and left the aircraft state unmonitored. The task order was restored only after the IP intervened verbally and directed which task to complete first, and the resulting deviations reached the limit of the acceptable standard. SP completed all tasks, but the sequence had to be imposed from outside.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the log entry before the turn was established, briefly allowed the workload at the turning point to compress. SP recognized the saturation, deferred the log entry, flew the turn accurately and then completed the remaining tasks in order without prompting. All required actions were completed and the aircraft state stayed inside the acceptable limits.
texts.3: SP put the cockpit tasks in order without missing anything significant, sequencing the turn, the fuel check, the log entry and the radio calls so that flying the aircraft was never displaced. Multiple tasks were handled in sequence rather than in parallel, and no channelized attention developed at any point of the route.
texts.4: SP managed the navigation workload so that each turning point was flown with the tasks already sequenced and spread before it arrived, leaving spare capacity at every stage. Additional demands from the IP and from ATC were absorbed without any degradation of aircraft control, and SP never approached the limit of available capacity.
texts.marginal: SP completed all required tasks within the standards, but the workload was consistently allowed to accumulate at the turning points instead of being spread before them. The trend was toward working at the edge of available capacity whenever an unplanned demand appeared. SP is expected to sequence and advance cockpit tasks so that spare capacity remains available at the busiest points of the route.

texts_at.1: SP prioritized cockpit tasks at the turning points inside the standard required at this stage, the task order restored only after the IP intervened and directed which task to complete first. The trend traces to the fuel check, the log entry and the position report being attempted simultaneously rather than sequenced. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to sequence those three tasks rather than attempt them together so the order does not need to be imposed.
texts_at.2: SP prioritized cockpit tasks at the turning points inside the standard required at this stage, workload briefly compressing when the log entry was started before the turn was established. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to defer the log entry until the turn is established so the workload does not compress at the start of it.
texts_at.3: SP put the cockpit tasks in order without missing anything significant, sequencing the turn, the fuel check, the log entry and the radio calls so flying the aircraft was never displaced, the small margin tracing to one sequence being reordered a beat after the turning point rather than planned before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to plan the sequence before every turning point so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the saturation, deferred the log entry, flew the turn accurately and then completed the remaining tasks in order without prompting, all required actions completed with the aircraft state staying inside the acceptable limits, after workload had briefly compressed at the start of a turn. Deferring the log entry until the turn is established from the start, rather than recognizing the compression afterward, would remove even that peak. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured task prioritization discipline.
texts_above.3: SP put the cockpit tasks in order without missing anything significant, sequencing the turn, the fuel check, the log entry and the radio calls so that flying the aircraft was never displaced, multiple tasks handled in sequence rather than in parallel. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise task prioritization discipline.
texts_above.4: SP managed the navigation workload so each turning point was flown with the tasks already sequenced and spread before it arrived, leaving spare capacity at every stage even when additional demands appeared from the IP or ATC. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate task prioritization discipline.

error_modes.label: FUEL, TIME AND RTB/DIVERT DECISION MAKING

texts.0: SP, due to failing to monitor fuel and elapsed time against the flight plan, arrived at the last turning point without any assessment of whether the route could be completed. No contingency or alternative was identified, no divert decision was stated and the aircraft continued toward the destination with the reserve already committed. The IP had to make and execute the recovery decision and to direct the return to base.
texts.1: SP, due to fuel and time checks made only at the destination leg rather than at each turning point, recognized the shortfall against the plan late. The decision to shorten the route and return to base was taken only after the IP prompted and stated the fuel position, and the aircraft landed with the reserve at the limit of the acceptable standard. The decision itself was correct once made, but it was neither timely nor self-initiated.
texts.2: SP, due to an initially optimistic estimate of the groundspeed on the first leg, planned to complete the full route with less margin than the conditions supported. SP identified the discrepancy at the fuel check on the second turning point, stated the revised assessment, shortened the last leg and returned to base with the planned reserve intact. The decision was made in time and required no IP input.
texts.3: SP monitored fuel and elapsed time against the plan at every turning point, identified contingencies and alternatives correctly and adjusted the execution of the navigation to make the best use of the remaining fuel and flight time. The decision to continue, shorten or divert was stated clearly with the rationale, and the aircraft returned to base with the planned reserve.
texts.4: SP kept a running comparison of fuel and time against the plan and revised the recovery picture continuously as actual winds and groundspeed became known. Alternatives and decision points were identified and stated before they were needed, the profile was adjusted to extract maximum training value from the available fuel and time, and the aircraft recovered with the reserve exactly as planned.
texts.marginal: SP monitored fuel and time and made a correct recovery decision within the required standards, but the assessment was made only when the figures were requested rather than as a continuous part of the navigation. The trend was toward reacting to the fuel state instead of anticipating it. SP is expected to state the recovery and divert picture at each turning point, before the situation forces the decision.

texts_at.1: SP made fuel, time and RTB or divert decisions inside the standard required at this stage, the decision to shorten the route taken only after the IP prompted and stated the fuel position. The trend traces to fuel and time checks being made only at the destination leg rather than at each turning point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to check fuel and time at every turning point so a shortfall against the plan is recognized without prompting.
texts_at.2: SP made fuel, time and RTB or divert decisions inside the standard required at this stage, an initially optimistic groundspeed estimate on the first leg identified as a discrepancy at the second turning point fuel check. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the groundspeed estimate against the actual figure at the first turning point so the discrepancy is identified sooner.
texts_at.3: SP monitored fuel and elapsed time against the plan at every turning point, identified contingencies and alternatives correctly and stated the decision to continue, shorten or divert with the rationale, the small margin tracing to one statement being given a beat after the decision rather than with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to state every decision at the moment it is made so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP identified the discrepancy at the fuel check on the second turning point, stated the revised assessment, shortened the last leg and returned to base with the planned reserve intact, after an initially optimistic groundspeed estimate on the first leg. Checking the groundspeed estimate against the actual figure at the first turning point, rather than identifying the discrepancy at the second, would remove even that delay. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent fuel and divert decision making.
texts_above.3: SP monitored fuel and elapsed time against the plan at every turning point, identified contingencies and alternatives correctly and adjusted the execution of the navigation to make the best use of the remaining fuel and flight time, the decision to continue, shorten or divert stated clearly with the rationale. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined fuel and divert decision making.
texts_above.4: SP kept a running comparison of fuel and time against the plan and revised the recovery picture continuously as actual winds and groundspeed became known, alternatives and decision points identified and stated before they were needed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to faultless fuel and divert decision making.

error_modes.label: CLEARING THE AIRSPACE AND SYSTEMS MONITORING WHILE A DISTRACTION APPEARS ON THE ROUTE

texts.0: SP, due to the absence of an aggressive disposition towards gaining and maintaining situational awareness, allowed an unexpected converging A/C and a system indication to become a complete distraction during a critical phase of the route. SP stopped clearing the airspace and stopped monitoring the A/C systems, so neither the traffic nor the aircraft state was being tracked while the leg continued. Separation from the converging traffic and the route parameters degraded beyond the acceptable limits and the IP took control to clear the aircraft and re-establish the navigation.
texts.1: SP, due to attention locking onto a caution indication shortly before a turning point, stopped clearing the airspace and did not visually acquire the converging A/C until the IP called it a second time. Lookout and systems monitoring were restored only after repeated verbal prompting, and the resulting closure and track error reached the limit of the acceptable standard. The indication itself was handled correctly, but the priority between flying, clearing and assessing the malfunction had to be imposed by the IP.
texts.2: SP, due to a momentary distraction while assessing an unexpected system indication on the leg, interrupted the lookout scan for several seconds. SP recognized the lapse without prompting, cleared the sector, acquired the reported traffic visually and resumed monitoring the A/C systems while continuing the planned track. The deviation stayed between the acceptable and the limiting values and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP kept clearing the airspace and monitoring the A/C systems while assessing an unexpected indication and while acquiring converging traffic, without allowing either to displace flying the aircraft. Situational awareness of self and aircraft in relation to the traffic and the route was maintained continuously and the distraction produced no significant deviation from the planned track, altitude or timing.
texts.4: SP absorbed the converging traffic and the system indication as routine events, keeping the lookout scan, the systems monitoring and the navigation running in parallel throughout. The traffic was acquired before it was called, the indication was assessed and reported without interrupting the leg, and the route parameters remained unaffected.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft within the required standards while handling the distraction, but the lookout scan and the systems monitoring visibly narrowed each time an unexpected event appeared. The trend was toward dealing with the event first and resuming clearing afterwards. SP is expected to maintain the clearing and monitoring pattern continuously, so that an unexpected malfunction or converging A/C is absorbed without a gap in situational awareness.

texts_at.1: SP kept clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems while a distraction appeared inside the standard required at this stage, lookout and systems monitoring restored only after repeated verbal prompting following an attention lock on a caution indication. The trend traces to the priority between flying, clearing and assessing the malfunction being decided during the event rather than fixed in advance. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to fix that priority order in advance so it does not need to be imposed during the event.
texts_at.2: SP kept clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems while a distraction appeared inside the standard required at this stage, the lookout scan interrupted for several seconds while an unexpected system indication was assessed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to assess an unexpected indication in short glances rather than a continuous interruption so the lookout scan is not fully displaced.
texts_at.3: SP kept clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems while assessing an unexpected indication and acquiring converging traffic, neither displacing flying the aircraft, the small margin tracing to the systems monitoring being resumed a beat after the traffic was acquired rather than together with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to resume both together so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the lapse without prompting, cleared the sector, acquired the reported traffic visually and resumed monitoring the aircraft systems while continuing the planned track, the deviation staying between the acceptable and the limiting values, after the lookout scan had been interrupted for several seconds by an unexpected indication. Assessing an unexpected indication in short glances from the start, rather than a continuous interruption followed by recovery, would remove even that lapse. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good distraction management technique.
texts_above.3: SP kept clearing the airspace and monitoring the aircraft systems while assessing an unexpected indication and while acquiring converging traffic, without allowing either to displace flying the aircraft, situational awareness maintained continuously with no significant deviation from the planned track, altitude or timing. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to very good distraction management technique.
texts_above.4: SP absorbed converging traffic and system indications as routine events, keeping the lookout scan, the systems monitoring and the navigation running in parallel throughout, traffic acquired before it was called and indications assessed without interrupting the leg. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to excellent distraction management technique.

error_modes.label: MISSION PREPARATION, BRIEFING AND EXECUTION AS BRIEFED

texts.0: SP, due to mission preparation that did not include study of the profile or of the rules and procedures governing the route, showed up unprepared to fly and could not discuss the navigation at the briefing. Questions on the profile were left unanswered and the mission requirements were not understood before engine start, so the sortie was flown without the intended plan. The route was not executed as briefed, the deviations exceeded the acceptable limits and the IP had to rebrief in the air and take control to complete the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete study of the profile before the briefing, was able to state the route but not the governing guidelines and the restrictions applying to it. Several elements of the plan were understood only after the IP repeated them verbally in flight, and the resulting departures from the briefed execution reached the limit of the acceptable standard. The mission was completed, but the briefed sequence had to be reinforced from outside the plan.
texts.2: SP, due to a preparation gap on one segment of the profile, initially flew that leg differently from the way it had been briefed. SP identified the discrepancy against the briefing notes, stated it, and returned to the briefed execution for the remainder of the route without prompting. The departure from the plan stayed short of the limiting values and required no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP arrived prepared to fly, having studied the profile and the applicable rules and procedures, was on time and ready to discuss the mission, and left no question unanswered at the briefing. The navigation was then executed as briefed and in accordance with the governing guidelines from engine start to engine shutdown, and the debriefing points were recognized by SP without being raised first by the IP.
texts.4: SP prepared the mission to a standard that allowed the entire profile, its restrictions and its contingencies to be briefed from memory and discussed in depth. Execution matched the brief precisely from engine start to engine shutdown, real time adjustments were made within the briefed framework rather than outside it, and SP led the discipline portion of the debriefing with accurate self-assessment.
texts.marginal: SP prepared and executed the mission within the required standards, but the preparation covered the sequence of the route more than the rules and procedures governing it. The trend was toward flying the plan correctly while being unable to justify it against the governing guidelines. SP is expected to prepare the rules and restrictions to the same depth as the profile, so that execution as briefed is a deliberate choice rather than a habit.

texts_at.1: SP prepared and executed the mission as briefed inside the standard required at this stage, several elements of the plan understood only after the IP repeated them verbally in flight. The trend traces to study before the briefing covering the profile but not the governing guidelines and restrictions applying to it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to study the governing guidelines to the same depth as the profile so elements do not need repeating in flight.
texts_at.2: SP prepared and executed the mission as briefed inside the standard required at this stage, one leg initially flown differently from the briefed sequence because of a preparation gap on that segment. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to close preparation gaps on every segment before the brief so no leg departs from the briefed sequence.
texts_at.3: SP arrived prepared to fly, having studied the profile and the applicable rules and procedures, and executed the navigation as briefed and in accordance with the governing guidelines from engine start to engine shutdown, the small margin tracing to one debriefing point being recognized a beat after the IP raised it rather than before. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to recognize every debriefing point before it is raised so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP identified the discrepancy against the briefing notes, stated it, and returned to the briefed execution for the remainder of the route without prompting, the departure from the plan staying short of the limiting values, after one leg had initially been flown differently because of a preparation gap. Closing that preparation gap before the brief, rather than identifying the discrepancy in flight, would remove even that departure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound mission preparation discipline.
texts_above.3: SP arrived prepared to fly, having studied the profile and the applicable rules and procedures, was on time and ready to discuss the mission, and left no question unanswered at the briefing, the navigation then executed as briefed from engine start to engine shutdown. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed mission preparation discipline.
texts_above.4: SP prepared the mission to a standard that allowed the entire profile, its restrictions and its contingencies to be briefed from memory and discussed in depth, execution matching the brief precisely from engine start to engine shutdown. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional mission preparation discipline.

error_modes.label: INTERRUPTED CHECKLIST NOT RESTARTED AT THE CORRECT POINT DURING THE ROUTE

texts.0: SP, due to an interruption from a radio call in the middle of a checklist on the leg, resumed at the point where the interruption was assumed to have occurred instead of restarting at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step. Items were omitted, a new checklist was started before the previous one had been completed, and completion was never positively confirmed. The omission left the aircraft configured incorrectly for the segment being flown and the IP had to stop the navigation, take control and run the checklist to restore the configuration.
texts.1: SP, due to resuming an interrupted checklist without backing up two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, omitted an item and did not detect the omission during the leg. The gap was identified only after the IP prompted, the checklist was then rerun, and the configuration error persisted long enough to place the affected parameter at the limit of the acceptable standard. Positive confirmation of completion was obtained, but only after external prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption during a checklist at a turning point, initially resumed one step after the interruption. SP recognized the risk of an omitted item, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step as required and positively confirmed completion before starting the next checklist. Nothing was omitted, the excursion in the affected parameter stayed inside the acceptable values and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP handled every checklist interruption during the route by restarting at the first step of the checklist or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, and positively confirmed completion before beginning the next one. No item was omitted, no new checklist was started before the previous one was complete, and the checklist work did not compete with flying the aircraft.
texts.4: SP planned the checklist work so that it fell between the high workload points of the route and was rarely interrupted at all. On the occasions when an interruption occurred, the restart point was applied without hesitation, completion was confirmed positively and the aircraft configuration matched the segment exactly at every stage.
texts.marginal: SP applied the correct restart point and omitted nothing, staying within the required standards, but checklists were repeatedly begun at the busiest points of the leg and therefore repeatedly interrupted. The trend was toward relying on the restart technique instead of protecting the checklist from interruption. SP is expected to start checklists where they can be completed without interruption and to keep the restart rule as the exception.

texts_at.1: SP handled checklist interruptions inside the standard required at this stage, an omitted item detected only after the IP prompted following a resumption that did not back up two to three steps. The trend traces to the checklist being resumed at the assumed next step rather than at the required restart point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to resume every interrupted checklist at the required restart point so items are not omitted.
texts_at.2: SP handled checklist interruptions inside the standard required at this stage, initially resuming one step after an interruption at a turning point before the correct restart point was applied. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to identify the restart point before resuming so the first attempt is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP handled every checklist interruption during the route by restarting at the first step or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, positively confirming completion before beginning the next one, the small margin tracing to one confirmation being given a beat after the checklist was closed rather than as it closed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to confirm completion as each checklist closes so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the risk of an omitted item, restarted two to three steps prior to the interrupted step as required and positively confirmed completion before starting the next checklist, nothing omitted and the excursion staying inside acceptable values, after initially resuming one step after an interruption. Identifying the restart point before resuming, rather than recognizing the risk after resuming incorrectly, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid checklist restart discipline.
texts_above.3: SP handled every checklist interruption during the route by restarting at the first step of the checklist or two to three steps prior to the interrupted step, and positively confirmed completion before beginning the next one, no item omitted and no new checklist started before the previous one was complete. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to well-developed checklist restart discipline.
texts_above.4: SP planned the checklist work so it fell between the high workload points of the route and was rarely interrupted at all, the restart point applied without hesitation on the occasions when an interruption occurred. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding checklist restart discipline.

error_modes.label: LIP SERVICE TO CHECKLIST ITEMS AND (BOTH) CHALLENGE AND RESPONSE

texts.0: SP, due to giving lip service to the checklist by calling the standardized phrase without actually performing the item or the required check, reported checklists complete while the associated switches and indications had never been verified. Items marked (BOTH) were treated as complete without challenging the PNF and without receiving a proper response, so no cross-cockpit verification existed at any point of the route. The aircraft was flown misconfigured for the segment beyond the acceptable limits and the IP took control and reran the checklists to establish the actual state.
texts.1: SP, due to reciting the mnemonic rather than performing each check behind it, reported a checklist complete with one item unverified and challenged a (BOTH) item without waiting for the response from the PNF. The discrepancy was found only when the IP questioned the item directly, and the resulting configuration error reached the limit of the acceptable standard before it was corrected. SP then reran the affected items correctly, but only under direct questioning.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried standardized call at a turning point, initially treated a (BOTH) item as complete before the response from the other cockpit had been received. SP recognized that the challenge and response had not been closed, repeated the challenge, obtained the proper response and positively confirmed the item before continuing. Nothing remained unverified and the deviation stayed short of the limiting values without IP input.
texts.3: SP performed each checklist item and the required check behind it rather than the phrase alone, and positively confirmed completion of every checklist regardless of how it was accomplished. Items marked (BOTH) were initiated as a challenge to the PNF and were treated as complete only after a proper response was received, so the cockpit configuration was verified on both sides throughout the route.
texts.4: SP performed and verified every checklist item deliberately, with the standardized phrase used only as the label for a check that had actually been carried out. Challenge and response on (BOTH) items was crisp and unhurried at every stage, completion was confirmed positively each time, and the aircraft configuration matched the briefed profile exactly for the whole navigation.
texts.marginal: SP performed the checklist items and confirmed completion within the required standards, but the pace of the standardized calls occasionally ran ahead of the check being performed and of the response from the other cockpit. The trend was toward the phrase leading the action rather than following it. SP is expected to slow the calls to the rate of the actual checks, so that no item and no (BOTH) response is ever assumed.

texts_at.1: SP performed checklist items and confirmed completion inside the standard required at this stage, a discrepancy on one (BOTH) item found only when the IP questioned it directly. The trend traces to the mnemonic being recited rather than the check behind it being performed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to perform the check behind every mnemonic so a discrepancy is found before it is questioned.
texts_at.2: SP performed checklist items and confirmed completion inside the standard required at this stage, one (BOTH) item initially treated as complete before the response from the other cockpit had been received. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to wait for the response before treating any (BOTH) item as complete so the first attempt is already correct.
texts_at.3: SP performed each checklist item and the required check behind it rather than the phrase alone, positively confirming completion of every checklist and treating (BOTH) items as complete only after a proper response, the small margin tracing to one response taking a beat longer to arrive than the rest. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to hold the same pace on every (BOTH) response so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized that the challenge and response had not been closed, repeated the challenge, obtained the proper response and positively confirmed the item before continuing, nothing left unverified, after initially treating a (BOTH) item as complete before the response arrived. Waiting for the response before treating any item as complete from the start, rather than recognizing the gap afterward, would remove even that correction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady checklist verification discipline.
texts_above.3: SP performed each checklist item and the required check behind it rather than the phrase alone, and positively confirmed completion of every checklist regardless of how it was accomplished, (BOTH) items treated as complete only after a proper response was received. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate checklist verification discipline.
texts_above.4: SP performed and verified every checklist item deliberately, the standardized phrase used only as the label for a check that had actually been carried out, challenge and response on (BOTH) items crisp and unhurried at every stage. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary checklist verification discipline.

error_modes.label: BINGO AND JOKER FUEL AT PRE-PLANNED TRANSITION POINTS OF THE NAVIGATION

texts.0: SP, due to omitting bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel from the mission brief, flew the route with no fuel gate at any pre-planned transition point and made no regular fuel checks. The bingo figure was passed without recognition and recovery was not initiated, so the aircraft continued toward the next turning point with the required arrival fuel already committed. The IP had to state the fuel state, direct the recovery and fly the aircraft back to the intended destination.
texts.1: SP, due to briefing a bingo fuel but no joker fuel for the transition points of the route, had no intermediate gate against which to assess progress and detected the bingo figure late. Recovery was initiated only after the IP stated the fuel remaining, and the aircraft arrived at the intended destination with the required fuel at the limit of the acceptable standard. The recovery itself was flown correctly, but the decision was neither self-initiated nor timely.
texts.2: SP, due to setting the joker fuel at a point that did not coincide with the planned transition between two segments, initially allowed the route to run past the intended decision point. SP identified the mismatch at the next regular fuel check, restated the joker figure against the actual transition point and adjusted the profile so that the bingo fuel was protected. The margin stayed inside the acceptable values and required no IP input.
texts.3: SP briefed bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel for the sortie, set the joker figures at the pre-planned transition points of the route and performed regular fuel checks throughout. Each joker gate was called and assessed as it was reached, the profile was adjusted where required, and the aircraft recovered to the intended destination with the required fuel intact.
texts.4: SP briefed bingo and multiple joker fuels matched to every transition of the profile and tracked the actual fuel against them continuously rather than only at the gates. Each gate was reached with the decision already prepared, the recovery was initiated ahead of bingo as the sortie duration required, and the aircraft arrived with the required fuel exactly as planned.
texts.marginal: SP briefed bingo and joker fuel and stayed within the required standards, but the joker gates were treated as figures to be read rather than as decision points to be acted on. The trend was toward passing a gate, noting it and continuing unchanged. SP is expected to state the decision associated with each joker fuel as it is reached, so that the bingo figure is never the first point at which the plan is reconsidered.

texts_at.1: SP briefed bingo and joker fuel at pre-planned transition points inside the standard required at this stage, the bingo figure detected late enough that recovery was initiated only after the IP stated the fuel remaining. The trend traces to a bingo fuel being briefed without a joker fuel for the transition points of the route. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to brief a joker fuel at every transition point so the bingo figure is not the first gate reached.
texts_at.2: SP briefed bingo and joker fuel at pre-planned transition points inside the standard required at this stage, one joker figure initially set at a point that did not coincide with the planned transition between two segments. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set every joker figure at the planned transition point itself so it does not need restating.
texts_at.3: SP briefed bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel for the sortie, set the joker figures at the pre-planned transition points and performed regular fuel checks throughout, each joker gate assessed as it was reached, the small margin tracing to one profile adjustment being made a beat after the gate rather than at it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to make every adjustment at the gate itself so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP identified the mismatch at the next regular fuel check, restated the joker figure against the actual transition point and adjusted the profile so the bingo fuel was protected, the margin staying inside acceptable values with no IP input, after one joker figure had initially been set away from the planned transition. Setting every joker figure at the planned transition point from the start, rather than restating it at the next check, would remove even that mismatch. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable fuel gate discipline.
texts_above.3: SP briefed bingo fuel and at least one joker fuel for the sortie, set the joker figures at the pre-planned transition points of the route and performed regular fuel checks throughout, each joker gate called and assessed as it was reached. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good fuel gate discipline.
texts_above.4: SP briefed bingo and multiple joker fuels matched to every transition of the profile and tracked the actual fuel against them continuously rather than only at the gates, each gate reached with the decision already prepared. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to superior fuel gate discipline.

error_modes.label: COCKPIT ORGANIZATION SCALED TO THE COMPLEXITY OF THE NAVIGATION SORTIE
error_modes.source: technique:8.5 TASK MANAGEMENT AND / OR COCKPIT ORGANIZATION

texts.0: SP, due to treating the navigation sortie with the same level of organization as a local instrument sortie, brought no additional preparation for a profile that combined an instrument portion, a VFR route and practice approaches at the destination. Charts, logs, approach plates and frequencies were neither sequenced nor accessible, so each phase transition was met with the material for the previous phase still in use. Preparation for upcoming tasks stopped entirely, the profile fell behind the aircraft beyond the acceptable limits and the IP took control to reorganize the cockpit and continue the sortie.
texts.1: SP, due to organizing the cockpit only to the level required for a local sortie, was unprepared for the transition from the VFR route to the approach phase and had to search for the required material after the transition had begun. The next phase was set up only after the IP prompted with the frequency and the plate, and the resulting delay placed the profile at the limit of the acceptable standard. All tasks were eventually completed, but nothing had been prepared in advance.
texts.2: SP, due to organization that matched the route but not the change of phase at its end, arrived at the last turning point without the arrival material prepared. SP recognized that the sortie had become more complex than the preparation allowed, used the remaining leg to sequence the plates and frequencies and entered the approach phase set up and on time. The delay stayed inside the acceptable values and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP applied the cockpit organization principles of the instrument sortie and added organization in proportion to the added complexity of the navigation profile. Material for each phase was prepared before the phase began, so the transitions between the instrument portion, the VFR route and the arrival were flown without any loss of position in the sequence.
texts.4: SP organized the cockpit so that each phase of the navigation was prepared well before it arrived, consistently finding ways to get ahead of the aircraft rather than keeping pace with it. Charts, logs, plates and frequencies were sequenced for the whole profile before takeoff and were revised in flight as the plan changed, so every phase transition was flown with spare capacity available.
texts.marginal: SP organized the cockpit sufficiently to stay within the required standards, but the preparation was completed just as each phase began rather than in advance of it. The trend was toward matching the pace of the sortie instead of getting ahead of it. SP is expected to prepare the material for the next phase while the current one is still routine, so that the added complexity of the navigation profile is absorbed before it is met.

texts_at.1: SP organized the cockpit in proportion to the complexity of the navigation sortie inside the standard required at this stage, the next phase set up only after the IP prompted with the frequency and the plate. The trend traces to the cockpit being organized to the level of a local sortie rather than to the added complexity of this one. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to organize the cockpit for the actual complexity of the sortie so the next phase is set up without prompting.
texts_at.2: SP organized the cockpit in proportion to the complexity of the navigation sortie inside the standard required at this stage, the arrival material not yet prepared on reaching the last turning point before the mismatch was recognized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to prepare arrival material a turning point earlier than it is needed so it is ready in time.
texts_at.3: SP applied the cockpit organization principles of the instrument sortie and added organization in proportion to the added complexity of the navigation profile, material for each phase prepared before the phase began, the small margin tracing to one transition being flown a beat before the material was fully set out rather than after. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to have the material fully set out before every transition so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized that the sortie had become more complex than the preparation allowed, used the remaining leg to sequence the plates and frequencies and entered the approach phase set up and on time, the delay staying inside acceptable values, after arrival material was not yet prepared on reaching the last turning point. Preparing arrival material a turning point earlier than needed, rather than recognizing the mismatch at the last one, would remove even that delay. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured cockpit organization technique.
texts_above.3: SP applied the cockpit organization principles of the instrument sortie and added organization in proportion to the added complexity of the navigation profile, material for each phase prepared before the phase began so the transitions between the instrument portion, the VFR route and the arrival were flown without any loss of position in the sequence. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to precise cockpit organization technique.
texts_above.4: SP organized the cockpit so each phase of the navigation was prepared well before it arrived, consistently finding ways to get ahead of the aircraft rather than keeping pace with it, charts, logs, plates and frequencies sequenced for the whole profile before takeoff. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate cockpit organization technique.

error_modes.label: OPERATIONS CHECKS EVERY 15-20 MINUTES AND UPDATE OF THE CLOSEST DIVERT FIELD

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the operations check from the route entirely, flew the navigation without any periodic review of fuel, systems and position and never updated the closest divert field as the route progressed. The divert field carried from the departure briefing remained unchanged for the whole sortie and bore no relation to the aircraft position at any later stage. When a divert was discussed the answer was unusable, the aircraft state had gone unmonitored beyond the acceptable limits and the IP took control to run the check and re-establish the recovery picture.
texts.1: SP, due to performing operations checks only when the workload allowed rather than at the required interval of every 15 to 20 minutes, left long stretches of the route unchecked and the closest divert field was not updated across two turning points. The check and the divert update were carried out only after the IP prompted, and the fuel and systems picture reached the limit of the acceptable standard before it was refreshed. The content of the check was correct once performed.
texts.2: SP, due to the workload at a turning point, allowed the operations check to slip past the required 15 to 20 minute interval. SP recognized the overdue check without prompting, completed it on the following leg and updated the closest divert field to match the actual position before the next turning point. The gap stayed inside the acceptable values and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP performed operations checks every 15 to 20 minutes throughout the navigation and updated the closest divert field at each one, so fuel, systems and the recovery option were reviewed against the actual position on a regular cycle. The checks were fitted into the route without displacing the timing, the landmark identification or the radio work.
texts.4: SP ran the operations check on the required cycle without any reminder and used each one to update the closest divert field, the fuel picture and the systems state against the aircraft position at that moment. The checks were positioned in the quiet parts of the legs, the divert field was current at every point of the route, and the cycle continued unaffected by changes to the plan.
texts.marginal: SP performed the operations checks at the required interval and stayed within the standards, but the closest divert field was updated only when the route made the change obvious. The trend was toward treating the check as a fuel and systems review rather than as a recovery review. SP is expected to update the closest divert field at every operations check, so that the recovery option matches the aircraft position at all times.

texts_at.1: SP performed operations checks and updated the closest divert field inside the standard required at this stage, the check and the divert update carried out only after the IP prompted, with two turning points passed unchecked. The trend traces to operations checks being performed when workload allowed rather than at the required 15 to 20 minute interval. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to run the check on the required interval regardless of workload so it does not fall behind.
texts_at.2: SP performed operations checks and updated the closest divert field inside the standard required at this stage, one check slipping past the required interval because of workload at a turning point before it was recognized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to protect the operations check from turning point workload so it does not slip past the interval.
texts_at.3: SP performed operations checks every 15 to 20 minutes throughout the navigation and updated the closest divert field at each one, fuel, systems and the recovery option reviewed against the actual position on a regular cycle, the small margin tracing to one update being made a beat after the check rather than with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to update the divert field at the same moment as the check itself so this small margin is removed.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the overdue check without prompting, completed it on the following leg and updated the closest divert field to match the actual position before the next turning point, the gap staying inside acceptable values, after one check had slipped past the interval because of turning point workload. Protecting the operations check from turning point workload from the start, rather than recognizing the slip afterward, would remove even that gap. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent operations check discipline.
texts_above.3: SP performed operations checks every 15 to 20 minutes throughout the navigation and updated the closest divert field at each one, so fuel, systems and the recovery option were reviewed against the actual position on a regular cycle without displacing timing, landmark identification or radio work. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined operations check discipline.
texts_above.4: SP ran the operations check on the required cycle without any reminder and used each one to update the closest divert field, the fuel picture and the systems state against the aircraft position at that moment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to faultless operations check discipline.

error_modes.label: WINGMAN CONTRACT - QUERY WHEN UNSURE, SPEAK UP, AND DO NOT ACT UNTIL DIRECTED
error_modes.source: technique:9.1 INTRODUCTION - PURPOSE, FLIGHT DISCIPLINE, AGGRESSIVENESS

texts.0: SP, due to a failure to meet the contractual obligations of the Number 2 role, acted before being directed by Number 1, accepted a directed task that was beyond the current ability without saying so, and did not query when unsure of the assigned position. The flight was allowed to continue toward an unauthorized segment of the route without SP speaking up, and the position parameters for the directed formation were not held. Mutual support was lost, the deviation exceeded the acceptable limits and the IP took control to reposition the aircraft and stop the sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to query Number 1 when the assigned position was unclear, remained out of the proper parameters for the directed position and made no radio call. The query was made only after the IP prompted and the correction to the briefed position was applied late, leaving the position error at the limit of the acceptable standard. SP responded correctly once directed, but the ambiguity was resolved from outside rather than by an immediate query.
texts.2: SP, due to an unclear directive during a turn at a turning point, was briefly uncertain of the assigned position and began to reposition before being directed. SP stopped the movement, queried Number 1 immediately, confirmed the position and then responded smoothly and in a timely manner. The excursion from the proper parameters stayed inside the acceptable values and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP flew within the proper parameters for the position directed by the flight lead, did not act until directed by Number 1 and then responded smoothly and in a timely manner. Where the assigned position or a directive was unclear, SP queried immediately rather than continuing, and stated clearly when a directed task was outside his or her current ability.
texts.4: SP held the directed position parameters throughout the navigation with no tolerance for remaining out of position, and every response to Number 1 was smooth, timely and correctly sequenced.
